description:
The promise of seeing God face to face introduces a new section of the Heaven study. Wesam Saad begins by recalling the previous discussion of the earth’s restoration, then presents God himself as the believer’s greatest reward. Before answering what seeing God means, he turns to Revelation 21 and 22 to establish the setting. The result is a study of the New Jerusalem and the presence of God within it.

Saad follows John’s description of the descending city, its gates, foundations, precious materials and divine light. He explains the absence of a temple in relation to the removal of sin and open access to God. He repeatedly distinguishes the city from the whole renewed earth: the city’s lack of need for sunlight is not, in his interpretation, a statement that the sun ceases to exist. The river, fruit and monthly cycle also contribute to his picture of continuing embodied life.

Questions from the group reveal details that remain unsettled, including who occupies the city and how its illumination relates to Christ’s activity. Saad postpones fuller treatment of these matters. The session prepares listeners to consider communion with God within a restored creation, while leaving its central face-to-face question for a later meeting.

questions.question: Why does the discussion of seeing God begin with the renewed earth?
questions.answer: Saad recalls the completed discussion of restoration before introducing the promise of seeing God. He explains that the physical setting helps listeners avoid imagining an undefined, disembodied trance. God himself is the reward, and the New Jerusalem supplies context for understanding that future fellowship.

questions.question: What does the descending New Jerusalem contribute to the study’s picture of heaven?
questions.answer: Saad draws attention to a city coming from God, with gates, foundations and carefully described materials. He reads this as part of the restored earth rather than an escape from creation. The description provides a concrete setting for the following discussion of God’s presence.

questions.question: Why does Saad say that the city has no temple?
questions.answer: He explains the temple’s separating function in relation to sin. In a place without sin, that separation is no longer needed. He interprets God and the Lamb being its temple as open access to God, rather than a requirement to enter a separate building to meet him.

questions.question: How does he distinguish the city’s illumination from conditions across the whole earth?
questions.answer: Saad stresses that the passage describes the New Jerusalem. He takes its lack of need for the sun and moon to mean that God’s glory and the Lamb provide its light, not that those celestial bodies no longer exist. He argues that conditions outside the city should not automatically be treated as identical.

questions.question: Why are the river, trees and monthly fruit significant to his interpretation?
questions.answer: The river of life and trees bearing fruit give substance to the future setting, while fruit appearing each month points to a continuing cycle. Saad uses these details to argue against treating the eternal state as the disappearance of ordinary created life and every form of temporal sequence.

questions.question: What role do the nations and their kings have in the discussion?
questions.answer: Saad observes that the nations walk by the city’s light and their kings bring glory and honour into it. He presents Jesus as King of kings, with the nations acknowledging his pre-eminence. Their presence also helps him distinguish the central city from the wider earth.

questions.question: Which questions does the session deliberately leave open?
questions.answer: Saad does not finish explaining what seeing God face to face means. He also defers the detailed question of the city’s inhabitants, acknowledges uncertainty about aspects of its materials and illumination, and says he has not fully assessed the proposed alternative reading of its measurements. These limits should not be turned into settled conclusions.
